los.text: Describe the key clinical features and examination findings in a patient presenting with tiredness and snoring.
los.html:
Obstructive sleep apnoea/hypopnoea syndrome (OSAHS)Repetitive upper airway collapse during sleep → apnoeas/hypopnoeas → arousals and desaturations → daytime symptoms.
Symptoms
  • Loud snoring
  • Witnessed apnoeas (partner)
  • Choking/gasping at night
  • Excessive daytime sleepiness (falling asleep in meetings, while driving)
  • Unrefreshing sleep
  • Morning headaches
  • Poor concentration/memory
  • Irritability/low mood
  • Nocturia
  • Reduced libido/erectile dysfunction
  • GORD.
Risk factors
  • Obesity (BMI >30; neck circumference >43 cm/17 in men)
  • Male sex
  • Age
  • Retrognathia/micrognathia
  • Enlarged tonsils/adenoids (children)
  • Macroglossia (acromegaly, hypothyroidism)
  • Nasal obstruction
  • Alcohol/sedatives at night
  • Smoking
  • FHx
  • Down syndrome
  • Pregnancy.
Examination
  • BMI
  • Neck circumference
  • BP (hypertension: OSA is a major cause of resistant HTN)
  • Oropharynx (crowded: Mallampati score, tonsils, large tongue, long soft palate)
  • Nasal patency (deviated septum, polyps)
  • Jaw position (retrognathia)
  • Signs of hypothyroidism/acromegaly
  • Signs of cor pulmonale/obesity hypoventilation (oedema, ↑JVP)
  • Lung exam.
Epworth Sleepiness Scale(0–24; >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness)Likelihood of dozing in 8 situations.
ConsequencesHypertension, AF, stroke, heart failure, T2DM, road traffic accidents (×2–7), depression, reduced quality of life.

los.text: Explain how clinical findings in a patient with tiredness and snoring can be used to formulate a differential diagnosis and outline initial management.
los.html:
Differential diagnosis of tiredness and snoring
  • OSAHS
  • Simple snoring (no apnoeas/sleepiness)
  • Obesity hypoventilation syndrome
  • Insufficient sleep/shift work
  • Depression
  • Hypothyroidism
  • Anaemia
  • Diabetes
  • Medications (sedatives, opioids, antihistamines)
  • Alcohol
  • Narcolepsy (cataplexy, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations)
  • Idiopathic hypersomnia
  • Restless legs/periodic limb movements
  • Central sleep apnoea (heart failure: Cheyne–Stokes; opioids)
  • Chronic fatigue
  • COPD overlap.
Initial investigations
  • Epworth score, STOP-BANG
  • Bloods (TFTs, FBC, HbA1c, U&E, venous bicarbonate (↑ suggests hypoventilation)), BP, sats
  • Home sleep study (respiratory polygraphy) or overnight oximetry → apnoea–hypopnoea index (AHI): mild 5–14, moderate 15–30, severe >30 events/h
  • Full polysomnography if unclear
  • ABG if hypoventilation suspected.
Initial management
  • Lifestyle: weight loss (± GLP-1 RA/tirzepatide), avoid alcohol/sedatives at night, smoking cessation, sleep position (positional OSA), sleep hygiene.
  • CPAP (first line for moderate–severe, or mild with symptoms: NICE NG202): splints airway open; improves sleepiness, BP, quality of life, driving safety.
  • Mandibular advancement device (mild OSA/snoring or CPAP intolerant); ENT surgery for specific obstruction (tonsillectomy in children), hypoglossal nerve stimulation (specialist).
Fitness to drive (DVLA)
  • Excessive sleepiness due to suspected/confirmed moderate–severe OSA (or mild with sleepiness) → must not drive and must notify DVLA
  • May resume once symptoms controlled on treatment (CPAP adherence confirmed)
  • Group 2 (HGV/bus) stricter (needs objective adherence).
  • Doctors must advise patients
  • If a patient continues to drive dangerously and won't inform DVLA → GMC allows disclosure to DVLA (inform patient first).

los.text: Apply knowledge of the control of ventilation to interpret arterial blood gases, including mixed acid–base disorders.
los.html:
Ventilatory control(see Y1 106)
  • Central chemoreceptors (CO₂/H⁺), peripheral chemoreceptors (↓ O₂ <8 kPa, ↑ CO₂, ↑ H⁺), medullary respiratory centres.
  • PaCO₂ is set by alveolar ventilation
  • PaO₂ by ventilation, V/Q matching, diffusion, FiO₂.
ABG interpretation steps
1. Oxygenation
  • PaO₂ (normal 10–13 kPa on air), relate to FiO₂ (expected PaO₂ ≈ FiO₂% − 10 kPa)
  • A–a gradient (↑ = V/Q mismatch, shunt, diffusion problem; normal in pure hypoventilation).
2. pHAcidaemia (<7.35) or alkalaemia (>7.45).
3. PaCO₂(4.7–6.0 kPa)Respiratory component.
4HCO₃⁻ (22–26) / base excess (±2): metabolic component.
5Compensation and whether mixed.
6Anion gap, lactate, glucose, K⁺, Na⁺, Cl⁻.
Respiratory failure
  • Type 1: PaO₂ <8 kPa with normal/low PaCO₂ (V/Q mismatch: pneumonia, PE, asthma, pulmonary oedema, ILD).
  • Type 2: PaO₂ <8 + PaCO₂ >6.0 (hypoventilation).
Acute vs chronic type 2
  • Acute → ↑ PaCO₂, ↓ pH, normal HCO₃⁻
  • Chronic → ↑ PaCO₂, normal pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻ (renal compensation over days)
  • Acute-on-chronic → ↑ PaCO₂, ↑ HCO₃⁻ but pH still low.
Mixed disorders(clues: compensation "too much/too little", normal pH with abnormal CO₂ and HCO₃⁻)
  • Respiratory + metabolic acidosis (cardiac arrest, severe pneumonia with sepsis/lactate; COPD + DKA) → very low pH, ↑ CO₂, ↓ HCO₃⁻.
  • Respiratory alkalosis + metabolic acidosis (salicylate poisoning, sepsis) → near-normal pH, ↓ CO₂ (more than expected), ↓ HCO₃⁻.
  • Metabolic alkalosis + respiratory acidosis (COPD on diuretics/steroids, vomiting).
  • Metabolic acidosis + metabolic alkalosis (DKA with vomiting: check anion gap vs HCO₃⁻).
Expected compensation
  • Metabolic acidosis → expected PaCO₂ (mmHg) = 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 (Winter's formula)
  • If PaCO₂ higher → coexistent respiratory acidosis.

los.text: Explain how pathological causes of hypoventilation lead to characteristic clinical features and inform management options.
los.html:
Hypoventilation↑ PaCO₂ (and ↓ PaO₂, normal A–a gradient) = type 2 respiratory failure.
Causes along the respiratory "chain"
LevelCauses
Central drive (brainstem)Opioids, benzodiazepines, alcohol, anaesthetics, brainstem stroke/tumour, raised ICP, central hypoventilation syndromes, hypothyroidism, excess O₂ in CO₂ retainers
Spinal cord/nervesHigh cervical cord injury (C3–5: phrenic), MND, Guillain–Barré, polio, phrenic nerve palsy
Neuromuscular junction/muscleMyasthenia gravis, Lambert–Eaton, botulism, muscular dystrophy (Duchenne), myopathies, hypokalaemia/hypophosphataemia
Chest wallKyphoscoliosis, flail chest, thoracoplasty, ankylosing spondylitis, obesity (obesity hypoventilation syndrome)
Airways/lungsCOPD (commonest), severe asthma (exhaustion), upper airway obstruction, bronchiectasis/CF (end stage), OSA overlap
Clinical features
  • Hypercapnia: headache (worse in morning), drowsiness/confusion → coma ("CO₂ narcosis"), flapping tremor, bounding pulse, warm peripheries, papilloedema
  • Hypoxia: cyanosis, tachycardia, confusion
  • Nocturnal hypoventilation: poor sleep, morning headaches, daytime sleepiness, orthopnoea (diaphragm weakness), cor pulmonale (oedema, ↑ JVP), polycythaemia
  • Weak cough → recurrent chest infections.
Investigations
  • ABG (↑ PaCO₂, ↑ HCO₃⁻ if chronic)
  • Venous bicarbonate
  • Lying and standing FVC (fall >20% supine = diaphragm weakness)
  • Mouth pressures/SNIP
  • Overnight oximetry/capnography
  • CXR
  • Neuro tests (NCS/EMG, AChR antibodies)
  • TFTs
  • Drug screen.
Management
  • Treat cause (naloxone for opioids, reverse sedation, treat myasthenic crisis (IVIg/plasma exchange), GBS)
  • Controlled O₂ (target 88–92%)
  • NIV (BiPAP) for acute and chronic hypercapnic failure (home NIV in neuromuscular disease, kyphoscoliosis, OHS, selected COPD)
  • Invasive ventilation if NIV fails/contraindicated
  • Airway clearance (cough assist)
  • Weight loss (OHS)
  • Ceilings of care discussions (MND).

los.text: Explain the pathophysiology of sleep apnoea and acute and chronic respiratory failure and how these relate to the clinical features and management.
los.html:
OSA pathophysiology
  • During sleep (especially REM), ↓ pharyngeal dilator muscle tone (genioglossus) + anatomically narrow/collapsible airway (fat deposition, large tonsils, retrognathia, ↓ lung volume in obesity)
  • → collapse
  • → apnoea (≥10 s cessation of airflow) or hypopnoea (≥30% ↓ with desaturation/arousal)
  • → hypoxaemia + hypercapnia
  • → ↑ respiratory effort against closed airway (↑ negative intrathoracic pressure)
  • → arousal (sympathetic surge)
  • → airway reopens
  • → loud snort
  • → cycle repeats (hundreds of times/night).
Consequences → clinical features
  • Sleep fragmentation → daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, mood change
  • Intermittent hypoxia + sympathetic activation → hypertension, AF, stroke, insulin resistance
  • Negative intrathoracic pressure → ↑ ANP → nocturia
  • ↑ afterload → heart failure.
Central sleep apnoea↓ respiratory drive (no effort): heart failure (Cheyne–Stokes respiration: unstable control loop due to prolonged circulation time), opioids, stroke, altitude.
Acute respiratory failure
  • Sudden failure of gas exchange: type 1 (V/Q mismatch, shunt: pneumonia, pulmonary oedema, ARDS, PE, asthma) or type 2 (ventilatory failure: COPD exacerbation, opioids, neuromuscular).
  • Features: breathlessness, tachypnoea, accessory muscles, cyanosis, confusion, drowsiness (CO₂), acidosis.
  • Management: treat cause
  • O₂ (targeted)
  • NIV (acidotic hypercapnic failure pH <7.35, PaCO₂ >6.5 after initial treatment)
  • CPAP (type 1: pulmonary oedema, COVID)
  • High-flow nasal oxygen
  • Intubation and ventilation.
Chronic respiratory failure
  • Gradual hypoventilation with renal compensation (normal pH, ↑ HCO₃⁻)
  • Polycythaemia, pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale, morning headaches, sleep disturbance.
  • Management: treat underlying disease
  • LTOT (type 1 or 2 with PaO₂ <7.3)
  • Home NIV (type 2: neuromuscular, OHS, chest wall disease, selected COPD with persistent hypercapnia after exacerbation)
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation
  • Vaccination
  • End-of-life planning.

los.text: Describe the principles of non-invasive respiratory support, including continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) and non-invasive ventilation (NIV).
los.html:
CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure)
  • Single constant pressure (typically 5–15 cmH₂O) throughout the respiratory cycle; not ventilation (doesn't directly reduce CO₂).
  • Mechanism: pneumatic splint for upper airway (OSA); recruits collapsed alveoli, ↑ FRC, improves V/Q and oxygenation, ↓ work of breathing; ↓ preload and afterload (cardiogenic pulmonary oedema).
  • Uses: OSA, type 1 respiratory failure (pulmonary oedema, COVID-19 pneumonitis, atelectasis), chest trauma.
NIV / BiPAP (bilevel positive airway pressure)
  • Two pressures: IPAP (inspiratory, e.g. 15–20+ cmH₂O) and EPAP (expiratory, e.g. 4–6 cmH₂O)
  • Pressure support = IPAP − EPAP → augments tidal volume → ↑ alveolar ventilation → ↓ PaCO₂
  • EPAP splints airway/offsets intrinsic PEEP.
  • Uses: acute hypercapnic (type 2) respiratory failure: COPD exacerbation with pH <7.35 and PaCO₂ >6.5 kPa despite optimal medical therapy (BTS: strong evidence ↓ mortality and intubation), neuromuscular disease, chest wall deformity, obesity hypoventilation; weaning; home NIV for chronic hypercapnia.
Contraindications/cautions
  • Untreated pneumothorax (drain first)
  • Facial trauma/burns
  • Upper GI surgery
  • Vomiting/bowel obstruction
  • Inability to protect airway/↓↓ GCS (relative)
  • Copious secretions
  • Haemodynamic instability
  • Patient refusal
  • Decide ceiling of treatment (intubation or not) before starting.
Practice
  • Tight-fitting mask (full face/nasal/hood)
  • Monitor sats
  • RR
  • Repeat ABG at 1–2 h and 4–6 h
  • Titrate pressures
  • Check leaks
  • Pressure sores
  • Aspiration
  • Patient comfort/anxiety
  • Continue until pH normalises
  • HDU/respiratory ward setting.
High-flow nasal oxygen (HFNO)Heated humidified O₂ up to 60 L/min, small PEEP effect, washes out dead space (type 1 failure).

los.text: Describe the current demographic changes and their effects on patterns of disease, healthcare provision and national economies.
los.html:
Demographic changes (UK)
  • Ageing population due to ↑ life expectancy (better living standards, medicine) and ↓ fertility (~1.4–1.5 births per woman, below replacement 2.1)
  • ~1 in 5 people aged ≥65 (higher in Wales, ~21%), fastest growth in ≥85
  • Post-war "baby boomers" entering old age
  • Old-age dependency ratio rising
  • Migration shapes age structure
  • Regional variation (rural Wales older).
Demographic transition modelHigh birth and death rates → falling death rates → falling birth rates → low both (ageing).
Effects on disease patterns
  • ↑ chronic diseases and multimorbidity (≥2 long-term conditions in most over-65s)
  • Dementia
  • Frailty
  • Falls
  • Cancer
  • CVD
  • Diabetes
  • Osteoarthritis
  • Sensory impairment
  • Polypharmacy
  • End-of-life care needs
  • "compression vs expansion of morbidity" debate (healthy life expectancy hasn't kept pace; widening inequalities).
Healthcare provision
  • ↑ demand on GP/hospitals (older people account for most bed days)
  • Delayed discharges (social care shortages)
  • Need for integrated health and social care
  • Community/home-based care
  • Geriatric medicine
  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment
  • Preventive care
  • Workforce pressures (and an ageing workforce)
  • Carers (unpaid carers ~£ billions of value).
National economies
  • ↑ dependency ratio (fewer working-age taxpayers per retiree)
  • ↑ pension and health/social care spending
  • Labour shortages
  • Raising state pension age
  • Reliance on migration
  • Productivity concerns
  • But older people also contribute (volunteering, grandparent childcare, consumer spending: "silver economy").
Policy responsesHealthy ageing strategies (Wales: Age Friendly Wales), prevention, technology/telecare, social care reform, pension reform.

los.text: Recognise the social, cultural, and biological aspects of death and dying.
los.html:
Biological aspects
  • Processes of dying (gradual decline in organ function, frailty trajectories)
  • Physical signs of approaching death (↓ intake, drowsiness, mottled skin, changes in breathing: Cheyne–Stokes, "death rattle" (secretions))
  • Biological death (irreversible cessation of circulation/respiration; brainstem death criteria in ICU)
  • Causes of death changing (from infectious to chronic disease; ~half of UK deaths in hospital).
Illness trajectories(Murray)Rapid decline (cancer), intermittent decline with exacerbations (organ failure: HF, COPD), prolonged dwindling (frailty, dementia).
Social aspects
  • Medicalisation and hospitalisation of death (most people would prefer to die at home)
  • "death-denying" society/taboo
  • Social death (loss of social roles before biological death; Sudnow)
  • Awareness contexts (Glaser & Strauss: closed, suspected, mutual pretence, open awareness)
  • The "good death" (control, comfort, dignity, preferred place, family present)
  • Inequalities in access to palliative care
  • Roles of family/carers
  • Funerals
  • Bereavement and grief (Kübler-Ross stages (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance: not linear); dual process model; continuing bonds).
Cultural/religious aspects
  • Beliefs about afterlife
  • Meaning of suffering
  • Truth-telling and family-centred disclosure
  • Rituals (Islam/Judaism: rapid burial, washing of body by same-sex family; Hinduism/Sikhism: cremation, chanting; Christianity: last rites)
  • Attitudes to post-mortems
  • Organ donation (Wales: opt-out system with family involvement)
  • End-of-life interventions
  • Expression of grief.
Clinical relevanceAdvance care planning, respecting preferences, culturally sensitive care after death (verification, certification, Medical Examiner system), supporting bereaved families, staff wellbeing.

los.text: See anatomy learning outcomes for week 208
los.html:
Pre-course session for ENT (week 208)
  • Preparation for the ENT week
  • The LOs for this session are the anatomy LOs listed under week 208 (Hearing and Balance) and the nose/sinus anatomy below.
Quick primer for 208
  • External ear (auricle, external acoustic meatus) → tympanic membrane → middle ear (malleus, incus, stapes; Eustachian tube; facial nerve and chorda tympani nearby) → inner ear (cochlea for hearing; vestibule (utricle, saccule) and semicircular canals for balance; CN VIII).
  • Facial nerve course (internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid) and branches.
  • Pharyngeal arches and derivatives.
  • Paranasal sinuses development and drainage.
See week 208 tab for full notes.

los.text: Name the parts of the external nose
los.html:
• External nose parts: root (between eyes), bridge (nasal bones), dorsum (ridge), tip/apex, columella (between nostrils), nares/nostrils (anterior apertures), alae (flared sides).
FrameworkComponents
Bony (upper third)Nasal bones, frontal processes of maxillae, nasal part of frontal bone
Cartilaginous (lower two-thirds)Upper lateral cartilages, lower lateral (alar) cartilages (medial and lateral crura), septal cartilage, accessory alar cartilages
Soft tissueFibrofatty alar tissue
Blood supplyFacial artery (lateral nasal, angular branches), ophthalmic artery (dorsal nasal, external nasal branch of anterior ethmoidal), infraorbital artery.
Venous drainage
  • Facial vein
  • → danger triangle of the face (upper lip/nose): communicates with cavernous sinus via ophthalmic veins (valveless)
  • → risk of cavernous sinus thrombosis from infection.
Sensory innervationV1 (infratrochlear, external nasal branch of anterior ethmoidal) and V2 (infraorbital).
ClinicalNasal bone fractures (commonest facial fracture: check septal haematoma), rhinophyma, basal cell carcinoma.

los.text: Name the bones that form the floor, roof and lateral walls of the nasal cavity and locate them on a model of a skull
los.html:
WallBones
RoofNasal bones, frontal bone (nasal spine), cribriform plate of ethmoid (olfactory nerve filaments; fracture → CSF rhinorrhoea, anosmia), body of sphenoid
FloorPalatine process of maxilla (anterior ¾) + horizontal plate of palatine bone (posterior ¼) = hard palate
Medial wall (nasal septum)Perpendicular plate of ethmoid (superior), vomer (posteroinferior), septal cartilage (anterior), plus crests of nasal/maxillary/palatine bones
Lateral wall
  • Maxilla (medial surface, with maxillary hiatus)
  • Ethmoid (labyrinth with superior and middle conchae)
  • Inferior concha (separate bone)
  • Lacrimal bone
  • Perpendicular plate of palatine bone
  • Medial pterygoid plate of sphenoid
  • Nasal bone
OpeningsAnterior nares (nostrils) and posterior choanae (into nasopharynx); sphenopalatine foramen (lateral wall posteriorly: vessels and nerves enter).
Skull model
  • Locate cribriform plate from inside the anterior cranial fossa
  • Vomer and perpendicular plate in midline
  • Conchae on lateral wall
  • Hard palate from below.

los.text: Describe the major landmarks on the lateral wall of the nose and the major arteries that supply the lateral wall and the nasal septum (in relation to nosebleeds)
los.html:
Lateral wall landmarks
  • Three conchae (turbinates) (superior and middle: ethmoid; inferior: separate bone) projecting medially
  • Meatuses beneath each
  • Spheno-ethmoidal recess above superior concha
  • Under middle concha: ethmoidal bulla (bulging middle ethmoid cells), semilunar hiatus (curved groove), uncinate process
  • Nasolacrimal duct opening in inferior meatus (valve of Hasner)
  • Sphenopalatine foramen posteriorly
  • Atrium/vestibule anteriorly (skin with hairs: vibrissae).
Arterial supply(both lateral wall and septum)
  • Sphenopalatine artery (terminal branch of maxillary artery, external carotid): main supply posteriorly (posterior lateral nasal branches and posterior septal branch) → posterior epistaxis (older, hypertensive, heavy bleeding).
  • Anterior and posterior ethmoidal arteries (from ophthalmic artery, internal carotid): roof, upper septum and lateral wall.
  • Greater palatine artery (maxillary): via incisive canal to anterior septum/floor.
  • Superior labial artery (facial): septal branch to anterior septum/vestibule.
Kiesselbach's plexus (Little's area)Anteroinferior septum where branches anastomose (sphenopalatine (septal), anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, superior labial) → site of ~90% of nosebleeds (anterior epistaxis: digital trauma, dry air, URTI).
Epistaxis management
  • First aid (sit forward, pinch soft part of nose for 10–15 min, ice), assess ABC and anticoagulants
  • Cautery (silver nitrate) to visible anterior bleeding point, nasal packing (Rapid Rhino), Naseptin cream (contains peanut oil)
  • Posterior bleeds → packing/balloon, ENT, sphenopalatine artery ligation (endoscopic) or embolisation
  • Anterior ethmoidal ligation
  • Treat hypertension/coagulopathy.

los.text: Label on a diagram: superior, middle and inferior conchae, spheno-ethmoidal recess, superior, middle and inferior meatus.
los.html:
Diagram labels (lateral nasal wall, from above down)
  • Spheno-ethmoidal recess: space above the superior concha, in front of the sphenoid; sphenoid sinus drains here.
  • Superior concha → superior meatus beneath it: posterior ethmoidal air cells drain here.
  • Middle concha → middle meatus: frontal sinus (via frontonasal duct), maxillary sinus and anterior ethmoidal cells drain into the semilunar hiatus; middle ethmoidal cells open on the ethmoidal bulla. The ostiomeatal complex (middle meatus drainage pathway) is key in sinusitis.
  • Inferior concha (largest; separate bone) → inferior meatus: nasolacrimal duct opens here.
Conchae function↑ surface area → warm, humidify and filter inspired air; cause turbulence (deposits particles); nasal cycle (alternating congestion of turbinates).
Mnemonic for drainage
  • "SPEM, Middle FAME, Inferior Nasolacrimal": Sphenoid → spheno-ethmoidal recess
  • Posterior Ethmoid → superior meatus
  • Middle meatus → Frontal, Anterior (and middle) Ethmoid, Maxillary
  • Inferior meatus → nasolacrimal duct.

los.text: Locate paranasal air sinuses (frontal, maxillary, ethmoidal and sphenoidal).
los.html:
• Paranasal sinuses: air-filled extensions of nasal cavity lined with respiratory (ciliated) mucosa; named after bones.
SinusLocationNotes
FrontalFrontal bone above orbits, behind superciliary archesAbsent/asymmetrical in some; develops after ~7 yrs
Maxillary (largest)Body of maxilla, below orbit, above upper teeth roots
  • Ostium high on medial wall (poor gravity drainage → sinusitis)
  • Related to orbit floor (blowout fracture), upper molar/premolar roots (dental infection → sinusitis; oroantral fistula), infraorbital nerve in roof
Ethmoidal (air cells: anterior, middle, posterior)Ethmoid labyrinth between nasal cavity and orbit (separated by thin lamina papyracea)Present at birth; infection spreads to orbit → periorbital/orbital cellulitis (children)
SphenoidalBody of sphenoid, below sella turcica (pituitary)Relations: optic nerve/chiasm, cavernous sinus and internal carotid laterally; route for transsphenoidal pituitary surgery
  • Functions: lighten skull, voice resonance, humidification, crumple zone protecting brain/eyes, mucus production.

los.text: Describe the drainage of the air sinuses and the nasolacrimal ducts and their relationships to the nasal cavities.
los.html:
StructureDrains into
Frontal sinusMiddle meatus (semilunar hiatus) via frontonasal duct/recess
Maxillary sinusMiddle meatus (semilunar hiatus)
Anterior ethmoidal cellsMiddle meatus (semilunar hiatus/ethmoidal infundibulum)
Middle ethmoidal cellsMiddle meatus (on/above ethmoidal bulla)
Posterior ethmoidal cellsSuperior meatus
Sphenoid sinusSpheno-ethmoidal recess
Nasolacrimal ductInferior meatus (anterior part), guarded by valve of Hasner
Mucociliary clearance
  • Cilia beat towards natural ostia (not gravity)
  • → blockage at ostiomeatal complex (middle meatus)
  • → stasis
  • → sinusitis of frontal, maxillary and anterior ethmoid sinuses together.
Nasolacrimal system
  • Tears → puncta → canaliculi → lacrimal sac (lacrimal fossa: lacrimal bone and maxilla) → nasolacrimal duct → inferior meatus.
  • Explains runny nose when crying
  • Congenital obstruction (watery eye in infants, valve of Hasner)
  • Dacryocystitis.
RelationsAll sinuses and the lacrimal system are closely related to the nasal cavity, orbit and cranial cavity → infection/tumour spread.

los.text: Explain the innervation of the paranasal sinuses in relation to referred pain.
los.html:
Sensory innervation of sinuses(all trigeminal)
  • Frontal sinus: supraorbital nerve (V1).
  • Ethmoidal cells: anterior and posterior ethmoidal nerves (V1, from nasociliary).
  • Sphenoid sinus: posterior ethmoidal (V1) and orbital branches of pterygopalatine ganglion (V2).
  • Maxillary sinus: infraorbital nerve and superior alveolar nerves (anterior, middle, posterior: V2).
Referred pain
  • Because sinuses share nerves with skin, teeth and other structures, sinus pain is felt elsewhere:
  • Maxillary sinusitis → cheek pain and upper teeth (molars/premolars) pain (superior alveolar nerves); and conversely dental infection can mimic sinusitis.
  • Frontal sinusitis → forehead pain/headache (supraorbital).
  • Ethmoidal sinusitis → pain between/behind the eyes, medial canthus.
  • Sphenoidal sinusitis → vertex, occipital or retro-orbital headache (deep, poorly localised).
Pain worse on bending forward; tenderness over affected sinus.

los.text: Discuss the nerve supply of the nasal cavity, including the olfactory nerves and the nerves of general sensation.
los.html:
Olfactory innervation
  • Olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity (upper septum, superior concha, under cribriform plate)
  • → bipolar olfactory receptor neurons
  • → axons (olfactory nerve, CN I, ~20 bundles) pass through the cribriform plate
  • → olfactory bulb
  • → olfactory tract
  • → olfactory cortex (piriform, entorhinal, amygdala; no thalamic relay).
  • Receptor neurons regenerate.
  • Anosmia: URTI (viral, COVID-19), head injury (shearing at cribriform plate), nasal polyps, Parkinson's/Alzheimer's (early sign), Kallmann syndrome, tumours (olfactory groove meningioma).
General sensation(trigeminal)
  • V1 (ophthalmic): anterior ethmoidal nerve (anterior superior septum and lateral wall; continues as external nasal nerve to tip of nose: Hutchinson's sign in shingles predicts eye involvement).
  • V2 (maxillary): via pterygopalatine ganglion through sphenopalatine foramen: nasopalatine nerve (septum → incisive canal), posterior superior lateral nasal nerves, greater palatine nerve (posterior inferior lateral wall), infraorbital (vestibule/external).
Autonomic
  • Parasympathetic from facial nerve (greater petrosal → nerve of pterygoid canal → pterygopalatine ganglion) → nasal glands (rhinorrhoea), vasodilation
  • Sympathetic (deep petrosal) → vasoconstriction (decongestants act here).
ClinicalSneeze reflex (trigeminal afferent), local anaesthesia for nasal procedures (topical on lateral wall/septum).

los.text: Recognise structures of the nasal cavities, air cavities and bones of the face on radiographs
los.html:
Plain radiographs of face/sinuses
  • Occipitomental (OM/Waters') view (15° and 30°): best for maxillary sinuses, orbits (floor), zygomatic arches, nasal cavity; also frontal sinuses.
  • Occipitofrontal (Caldwell) view: frontal and ethmoid sinuses.
  • Lateral view: sphenoid and frontal sinuses (depth), nasal bones, sella turcica, nasopharyngeal soft tissue (adenoids in children).
IdentifyNasal septum, inferior conchae, maxillary sinuses (dark, air-filled; compare symmetry), orbits, zygomatic arches and bodies, infraorbital margins, frontal sinuses, mandible, teeth.
Abnormalities
  • Sinus opacification/air–fluid level (acute sinusitis, haemosinus after trauma)
  • Mucosal thickening
  • Polyps
  • "teardrop sign" (orbital floor blowout fracture: herniated orbital contents into maxillary sinus roof)
  • Zygomatic complex fractures (step in infraorbital margin, separation of zygomaticofrontal suture)
  • Nasal bone fractures
  • Le Fort fractures.
Now mostly CT (sinus disease, pre-op FESS, trauma) and MRI (tumours); plain films have limited role.
